query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with an FCC matrix under elevated-temperature exposure is primarily governed by the stability and integrity of a protective oxide scale (predominantly Al2O3 and TiO2) that forms on its surface. In oxidizing atmospheres, a nominally protective scale initially slows degradation; however, if the scale becomes discontinuous or spalls (especially near vulnerable grain boundaries), rapid internal oxidation and embrittlement lead to catastrophic failure. In reducing atmospheres, the inhibition of robust oxide formation accelerates degradation by enhancing element diffusion along grain boundaries and promoting internal phase instability.
generation.material_initial_state: As-fabricated, additively manufactured high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous FCC matrix and as-developed grain boundary structure.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the gas environment by controlling oxygen (and/or H2) partial pressures during elevated-temperature exposure, thereby switching between oxidizing and reducing conditions.
generation.conditions: Exposures at elevated temperatures (e.g., above 600°C) for extended durations in controlled atmospheres: one set with a high oxygen partial pressure (oxidizing) and another with a low oxygen/ high reducing gas content.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and subsequent integrity (or failure) of the protective surface oxide scale, particularly at grain boundaries where discontinuities would enhance oxygen ingress and drive internal oxidation.
generation.mechanism: Under oxidizing conditions, the intended formation of a continuous Al2O3/TiO2 scale initially limits oxygen diffusion; however, eventual scale spallation or cracking introduces localized regions of accelerated oxidation, promoting intergranular degradation. Under reducing conditions, the absence or instability of this passivating layer facilitates more direct elemental diffusion and microstructural alteration, contributing to a rapid loss of mechanical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: When the oxygen partial pressure is increased, samples will initially show slower degradation due to protective scale formation but will later exhibit rapid degradation and catastrophic failure once the scale integrity is compromised. Conversely, under a reducing atmosphere, samples will experience a faster onset of microstructural instability and embrittlement owing to the lack of a stable protective scale, even without the scale spallation process.
generation.baseline: As-manufactured alloy with an initially homogeneous FCC microstructure and a naturally formed, continuous thin oxide film under ambient conditions before any elevated-temperature gas exposure.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to exposure conditions above approximately 600°C and under either sustained oxidizing or reducing gas atmospheres; it might not hold at lower temperatures or in mixed/transitioning atmospheres where oxide scale behavior can differ.
generation.uncertainty: The precise roles and relative contributions of alloying elements (especially Al and Ti) in maintaining or undermining the protective scales under fluctuating gas compositions are not fully quantified. The exact temperature/time thresholds for scale spallation and subsequent catastrophic structural failure are also uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy samples and expose them to controlled gas environments at temperatures >600°C. Divide the samples into two groups: one under a high oxygen partial pressure (oxidizing atmosphere) and another under a reducing atmosphere (e.g., with added H2 or low O2). Monitor the evolution of the surface oxide scale (using scanning electron microscopy and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy) and perform mechanical tests (e.g., fracture toughness or tensile tests) concurrently over time.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and continuity (by SEM/EDS)
Grain boundary oxidation levels (by high-resolution microscopy)
Time to onset of catastrophic failure (e.g., crack propagation measurement)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If systematic differences in degradation modes (oxide scale degradation, internal oxidation, and catastrophic failure) are not observed between the oxidizing and reducing conditions, or if the catastrophic failure does not correlate with the disruption of the protective oxide scale as predicted, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
In this study, the synergistic tuning mechanism of heat treatment (600, 800, and 1000 °C) and dealloying (40, 60, and 80 °C) on the microstructure and electrocatalytic performance of an FCC + BCC-type CoCrNi0.5Ti0.3V0.2Al0.4 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was systematically investigated. The findings indicate that with an increase in heat treatment temperature, there is a gradual increase in grain size and a change in the fraction of the two phases. Notably, heat treatment at 800 °C resulted in an FCC-dominated dual-phase structure with uniformly refined grains. As the dealloying temperature increased, the pore size also increased, leading to a uniform distribution of the internal FCC and BCC phases. The sample subjected to heat treatment at 800 °C and dealloying at 80 °C exhibited an OER overpotential of only 265 mV and a Tafel slope of 67.84 mV/dec, significantly enhancing the electrocatalytic activity and stability of the alloy. ## Abstract
AbstractIn the present study, AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was fabricated by laser melting deposition (LMD). Then, post-heat treatment was performed at different temperatures to investigate its effects on microstructure and corrosion property of the alloy. The results obtained from microstructural characterization indicate that the alloy, whether heat-treated or not, exhibited a lamellar eutectic microstructure composed of alternating FCC and BCC phases. With the increase in the heating temperature from 600 to 1000 °C, the interlamellar spacing and volume fraction of the FCC phase gradually increased. Electrochemical testing in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution revealed that the resistance of the alloy to corrosion was improved with the increasing heating temperature, which was attributed to the increased volume fraction of the FCC phase.
